claims.sentence: An X-ray uses a beam of electromagnetic radiation to make an image of the inside of the body.
claims.evidence: North Cumbria leaflet: X-ray imaging uses a beam of electromagnetic radiation.

claims.sentence: According to the NHS, X-rays can produce images of many parts of the body, including bones, teeth, lungs and the digestive system.
claims.evidence: NHS: X-rays image bones, teeth, lungs and the digestive system.

claims.sentence: They are used, for example, to check for broken bones after an accident.
claims.evidence: NHS: used to detect problems such as bone fractures.

claims.sentence: A trust leaflet says that specially trained staff check each request first, to confirm the test is the right one for the person and their condition.
claims.evidence: Search could not confirm 'specially trained staff check each request'.

claims.sentence: The health professional who takes X-rays in hospital is called a radiographer.
claims.evidence: NHS: radiographers are the trained staff who take the images.

claims.sentence: The radiographer positions the person sitting, lying or standing, depending on the part of the body.
claims.evidence: Newcastle trust: staff may ask you to sit, lie down or stand depending on the part examined; NHS says the radiographer may ask you to move into different positions.

claims.sentence: The X-ray itself takes only a few minutes, according to the NHS.
claims.evidence: NHS: the X-ray itself should only take a few minutes.

claims.sentence: The NHS says people are asked to remove metal items such as jewellery and zips.
claims.evidence: NHS: avoid wearing jewellery and clothes containing metal such as zips, as these will need to be removed.

claims.sentence: Some types need fasting for several hours beforehand.
claims.evidence: A trust says for some specific examinations people are told in advance to avoid eating and drinking for a few hours.

claims.sentence: The NHS lists several related tests, including angiography, which checks blood vessels using a dye injected into the blood.
claims.evidence: NHS: angiography checks blood vessels using a dye injected into the blood.

claims.sentence: It also lists DEXA scans, which measure bone density, and CT scans, which give more detailed images.
claims.evidence: NHS: DEXA measures bone strength; CT gives more detailed images.

claims.sentence: Studies of the digestive system use a barium drink or enema, a liquid that shows up on X-ray.
claims.evidence: NHS: barium swallow involves drinking barium; barium enema puts barium into the bowel via the rectum.

claims.sentence: After a dye or barium test, the NHS says people may be asked to wait for up to 30 minutes so staff can check for a reaction.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text mentions a 30 minute wait after dye or barium.

claims.sentence: The NHS says X-rays are safe and serious complications are rare.
claims.evidence: NHS page retrieved says the cancer risk is thought to be very small and a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects; words 'safe' and 'serious complications are rare' not found.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects and the cancer risk is thought to be very small.

claims.sentence: It adds that there is a very small risk of cancer linked to having lots of X-rays.
claims.evidence: NHS: cancer risk thought to be very small; link to 'lots of X-rays' not found in retrieved NHS text.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says the risk of cancer from X-rays is thought to be very small.

claims.sentence: Trust leaflets say staff keep doses as low as possible and that a test goes ahead only when its benefit outweighs the small risk.
claims.evidence: Worcestershire: doses kept as low as reasonably practicable; Cornwall and Bath leaflets: benefit should outweigh the risk.

claims.sentence: GOV.UK safety advice says that when imaging is properly justified and optimised, the risks from X-ray examinations are far smaller than the risks of the conditions being investigated.
claims.evidence: GOV.UK: when properly justified and optimised, risks are much less than the risks of the conditions being investigated.

claims.sentence: It describes the added chance of cancer as very small, and says any effect would appear years or decades later.
claims.evidence: GOV.UK retrieved: cancers take decades to appear, especially relevant for older patients; 'very small' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: GOV.UK safety advice says cancers linked to radiation can take decades to appear.

claims.sentence: The same advice says children have a higher lifetime risk from X-rays than adults, and that risk is lower for older patients because cancers take a long time to develop.
claims.evidence: GOV.UK: children have an increased lifetime risk depending on age and sex; risks lower for older patients since cancers take decades.

claims.sentence: These leaflets give their own figures for the risk, and the figures differ between leaflets, so the radiographer or the doctor who requested the test is the person to ask.
claims.evidence: Not retrieved that figures differ; instruction on who to ask is not sourced.

claims.sentence: Trusts ask anyone who might be pregnant to tell the team before an X-ray.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: most leaflets ask people to tell staff if they might be pregnant.

claims.sentence: A Leicester hospitals leaflet says X-rays during pregnancy do not increase the risk of miscarriage, birth defects or developmental problems.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: NHS leaflets say X-rays in pregnancy do not raise miscarriage risk and do not cause birth defects at typical doses; Leicester attribution not exact.
claims.newSentence: NHS trust leaflets say X-rays during pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage and, at typical doses, do not cause birth defects.

claims.sentence: The main concern it names is a very small increase in the chance that the baby develops cancer in childhood.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: main concern is a very small increase in childhood cancer risk (Leicester).

claims.sentence: X-rays of the abdomen and pelvis are usually avoided in pregnancy.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: tummy X-rays need special care; 'usually avoided' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Trust leaflets say X-rays of the tummy or near the womb need special care during pregnancy.

claims.sentence: X-rays of parts of the body well away from the abdomen, such as arms and legs, and dental X-rays, do not give any increased risk to an unborn baby, according to the same leaflet.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: a trust leaflet says X-rays away from the tummy, such as head, chest, arms or lower legs, are OK. Dental not confirmed; 'do not give any increased risk' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A trust leaflet says X-rays of parts of the body away from the tummy, such as the head, chest, arms or lower legs, are fine to have during pregnancy.

claims.sentence: When an urgent test is needed, a radiologist and the doctor who asked for it decide together whether it should go ahead.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: a test may go ahead in pregnancy if the health benefit clearly outweighs the small risk to the baby.
claims.newSentence: A test may go ahead during pregnancy if the health benefit clearly outweighs the small radiation risk to the baby.

claims.sentence: A reporting radiographer or a radiologist, a doctor who specialises in imaging, reviews the X-ray.
claims.evidence: NHS: images go to a radiologist or specially trained radiographer who reports.

claims.sentence: The report goes to the team that requested the test.
claims.evidence: Reports go back to the referring clinician.

claims.sentence: The NHS says results may come on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later, and that a clinician should explain them.
claims.evidence: NHS: results may be the same day or at an appointment a few weeks after; a healthcare professional should explain them.

claims.sentence: The wait varies with how urgent the X-ray is.
claims.evidence: Trust pages quote different waits (about ten working days to two weeks); urgency link not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Trusts quote different waits for the report, so timings differ between hospitals.

claims.sentence: An X-ray can produce images of many parts of the body, and the NHS lists fractures, teeth, lungs and the digestive system among them.
claims.evidence: As claims 2 and 3.

claims.sentence: The NHS describes X-rays as safe, with serious complications rare and a very small cancer risk linked to having lots of them.
claims.evidence: As claims 14 and 15: 'safe' and 'serious complications rare' not confirmed in retrieved NHS text.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects and the cancer risk is thought to be very small.

claims.sentence: Trust leaflets say X-rays in pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage or birth defects, and that those of the abdomen and pelvis are usually avoided.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: no miscarriage increase and no birth defects at typical doses; tummy X-rays need special care. 'Usually avoided' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Trust leaflets say X-rays during pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage, and that X-rays of the tummy or near the womb need special care.

claims.sentence: Results may be given on the same day or at an appointment some weeks later, depending on the type of X-ray.
claims.evidence: NHS says results may be the same day or at an appointment a few weeks after; dependence on type of X-ray not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says results may be given on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later.

claims.sentence: An X-ray uses a small beam of radiation to picture bones, lungs and other parts. This guide covers the test, radiation risk, pregnancy and results.
claims.evidence: NHS and leaflets: X-rays image bones, lungs and other parts; radiation risk, pregnancy and results are covered. Second sentence is a contents summary.

notes: Extra facts: (1) NHS says a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects and people can return to normal activities straight away (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/x-ray/). (2) NHS notes whitish stools for a few days after barium (same page). (3) UK joint position statement says pregnant patients should get relevant imaging while minimising radiation (https://www.rcr.ac.uk/news-policy/latest-updates/imaging-in-pregnancy-for-the-diagnosis-and-staging-of-suspected-cancer-joint-position-statement/). Dental X-ray safety in pregnancy and the 30-minute wait after dye were not found. Search results arrive as summaries, not verbatim page text.
